title: AC Power
description: Average, reactive, apparent and complex power, power factor correction and maximum power transfer.

study.title: Instantaneous and average power
study.body: The instantaneous power $p(t) = v(t)\,i(t)$ oscillates at twice the signal frequency. Its average depends on the **power angle** $\theta = \theta_v - \theta_i$, which equals the angle of the load impedance. Note the factor $\tfrac12$ when you use peak values; with rms values it disappears. Drag $\theta$ ($V_m$ = 10 V, $I_m$ = 2 A): at $0^\circ$ $p(t)$ never goes negative; towards $\pm 90^\circ$ it dips below zero for longer (energy flows back to the source) and the average falls to zero.

study.title: Power factor
study.body: $PF = \cos\theta$, often given as a percentage. If the current lags the voltage (inductive load, $\theta > 0$) the power factor is **lagging**; if it leads (capacitive load, $\theta < 0$) it is **leading**. A resistor has PF = 1; an ideal L or C has PF = 0 and absorbs no average power.

study.title: Reactive and apparent power
study.body: **Reactive power** $Q = V_{rms}I_{rms}\sin\theta$, in VAR, measures energy swapped back and forth with inductances and capacitances each cycle: positive for inductive loads, negative for capacitive ones. **Apparent power** $V_{rms}I_{rms}$, in VA, sets the current rating of cables and transformers. For a load $Z = R + jX$: $P = I_{rms}^2R$ and $Q = I_{rms}^2X$ (keep the sign of $X$).

study.title: Complex power and the power triangle
study.body: With peak phasors, the complex power is $\mathbf{S} = \tfrac12\mathbf{V}\mathbf{I}^*$ (with rms phasors, $\mathbf{V}_{rms}\mathbf{I}_{rms}^*$). Its real part is $P$, its imaginary part is $Q$, and its magnitude is the apparent power: a right triangle with angle $\theta$. For several loads, add the $P$'s and the $Q$'s separately; apparent powers generally do **not** add.

study.title: Power-factor correction
study.body: Industrial loads are mostly inductive (lagging). A capacitor in parallel with the load supplies negative $Q$, so the line carries less reactive power and less current, while the load's $P$ is unchanged. Recipe: $Q_{old} = P\tan\theta_{old}$, $Q_{new} = P\tan\theta_{new}$, $Q_C = Q_{new} - Q_{old} < 0$, and a capacitor absorbs $Q_C = -\omega C V_{rms}^2$.

study.title: Maximum power transfer
study.body: A source with Thévenin impedance $Z_t = R_t + jX_t$ delivers the most average power to a load that can take any value when $Z_L = Z_t^* = R_t - jX_t$: the reactances cancel and $R_L = R_t$. Then $P_{max} = |\mathbf{V}_t|^2/(8R_t)$ with a peak phasor $\mathbf{V}_t$, i.e. $V_{t,rms}^2/(4R_t)$. If the load must be a pure resistance, the best choice is $R_L = |Z_t|$.

steps.title: Average power
steps.body: Only the part of the current in phase with the voltage delivers net energy. With $\theta = \theta_v - \theta_i$ (the power angle), the average power uses rms values, or peak values with a factor $\tfrac12$.

steps.prompt: $v(t) = {{Vm}}\cos(\omega t + {{tv}}^\circ)$ V and $i(t) = {{Im}}\cos(\omega t + ({{ti}}^\circ))$ A (passive reference configuration). Find the average power absorbed.
steps.explanation:
$\theta = \theta_v - \theta_i = {{tv}}^\circ - ({{ti}}^\circ) = {{tv-ti}}^\circ$.
$P = \frac{V_mI_m}{2}\cos\theta = \frac{ {{Vm}}\times{{Im}} }{2}\cos({{tv-ti}}^\circ)$ = {{Vm*Im/2*cos(rad(tv-ti))|W}}.

steps.prompt: What average power does an ideal inductor absorb in sinusoidal steady state?
steps.explanation: In an inductor the current lags the voltage by $90^\circ$, so $P = V_{rms}I_{rms}\cos 90^\circ = 0$. Energy flows in during half of each cycle and back out during the other half. The same holds for an ideal capacitor ($\theta = -90^\circ$).

steps.title: Try it: the power angle
steps.body: Here $v = 10\cos(\omega t)$ V and $i = 2\cos(\omega t - \theta)$ A. Drag $\theta$. The power always pulses at twice the signal frequency with the same swing, but its **average** $P = \frac{V_mI_m}{2}\cos\theta$ moves: the full 10 W in phase, zero for a pure inductance ($+90^\circ$) or capacitance ($-90^\circ$).

steps.title: Power factor
steps.body: $PF = \cos\theta$. Inductive loads (current lags): **lagging** PF. Capacitive loads (current leads): **leading** PF. A low power factor means more current for the same useful power.

steps.prompt: Find the power factor (as a decimal) of a load with impedance $Z = {{R}} + j({{X}})$ Ω.
steps.explanation: $|Z| = \sqrt{ {{R}}^2 + ({{X}})^2} = {{sqrt(R^2+X^2)}}$ Ω, so $PF = \cos\theta = \frac{R}{|Z|} = \frac{ {{R}} }{ {{sqrt(R^2+X^2)}} } = {{R/sqrt(R^2+X^2)}}$, i.e. {{100*R/sqrt(R^2+X^2)|%}}. The angle is $\theta = {{deg(atan(X/R))}}^\circ$: lagging if $X > 0$ (inductive), leading if $X < 0$ (capacitive).

steps.prompt: A load has $Z = {{R}} - j{{X}}$ Ω. Its power factor is:
steps.explanation: Negative reactance means capacitive: $\theta = \arctan(-{{X}}/{{R}}) = {{-deg(atan(X/R))}}^\circ < 0$, so the current leads the voltage and the power factor $\cos\theta = {{R/sqrt(R^2+X^2)}}$ is **leading**.

steps.title: Q, apparent power and the triangle
steps.body: **Reactive power** $Q = V_{rms}I_{rms}\sin\theta$ (VAR) is positive for inductive and negative for capacitive loads. **Apparent power** $V_{rms}I_{rms}$ (VA) is the hypotenuse of the power triangle with legs $P$ and $Q$.

steps.prompt: A load absorbs $P$ = {{P|W}} and $Q$ = {{Q|VAR}}. Find its apparent power.
steps.explanation: $|\mathbf{S}| = \sqrt{P^2 + Q^2} = \sqrt{ {{P}}^2 + ({{Q}})^2}$ = {{sqrt(P^2+Q^2)|VA}}. The power factor is $P/|\mathbf{S}|$ = {{P/sqrt(P^2+Q^2)}}.

steps.prompt: Match each quantity to its unit.
steps.explanation: All three powers are physically volts × amperes, but different unit names tell you which one is meant: watts for average power, VAR for reactive power, VA for apparent power. The power factor is a ratio, $P/|\mathbf{S}|$.

steps.prompt: A current of {{I}} A rms flows through $Z = {{R}} + j{{X}}$ Ω. Find the reactive power $Q$ absorbed.
steps.explanation: $Q = I_{rms}^2X = {{I}}^2\times{{X}}$ = {{I^2*X|VAR}} (positive: inductive). Similarly $P = I_{rms}^2R$ = {{I^2*R|W}}. Only the reactance enters $Q$, only the resistance enters $P$.

steps.prompt: A {{V}} V rms source feeds the load $Z = {{R}} + j({{X}})$ Ω. Find the average power absorbed by the load.
steps.explanation:
$|Z| = \sqrt{ {{R}}^2 + ({{X}})^2} = {{sqrt(R^2+X^2)}}$ Ω, so $I_{rms} = {{V}}/{{sqrt(R^2+X^2)}}$ = {{V/sqrt(R^2+X^2)|A}}.
$P = I_{rms}^2R$ = {{V^2*R/(R^2+X^2)|W}}. Careful: $V_{rms}^2/R$ would be wrong here, because the full source voltage is not across the resistance.

steps.prompt: A current of {{I}} A rms flows through $Z = {{R}} - j{{Xc}}$ Ω. Find the reactive power $Q$ absorbed, with its sign.
steps.explanation: $Q = I_{rms}^2X$ with $X = -{{Xc}}$ Ω: $Q = {{I}}^2\times(-{{Xc}})$ = {{-I^2*Xc|VAR}}. Capacitive loads absorb negative reactive power, i.e. they **supply** reactive power.

steps.prompt: A load absorbs {{P|W}} at a power factor of {{pf}} lagging. Find its reactive power $Q$.
steps.explanation: $\theta = \arccos({{pf}}) = {{deg(acos(pf))}}^\circ$ (positive, because lagging). From the power triangle, $Q = P\tan\theta = {{P}}\times\tan({{deg(acos(pf))}}^\circ)$ = {{P*tan(acos(pf))|VAR}}. The apparent power is $P/PF$ = {{P/pf|VA}}.

steps.prompt: A load has (peak) phasors $\mathbf{V} = {{Vm}}\angle {{tv}}^\circ$ V and $\mathbf{I} = {{Im}}\angle {{ti}}^\circ$ A. Find its reactive power $Q$, with sign.
steps.explanation:
$\mathbf{S} = \tfrac12\mathbf{V}\mathbf{I}^* = \tfrac12({{Vm}}\angle {{tv}}^\circ)({{Im}}\angle {{-ti}}^\circ) = {{Vm*Im/2}}\angle {{tv-ti}}^\circ$ VA.
$Q = \mathrm{Im}(\mathbf{S}) = {{Vm*Im/2}}\sin({{tv-ti}}^\circ)$ = {{Vm*Im/2*sin(rad(tv-ti))|VAR}} and $P$ = {{Vm*Im/2*cos(rad(tv-ti))|W}}.

steps.prompt: Load A absorbs {{P1|W}} and {{Q1|VAR}}; load B, in parallel, absorbs {{P2|W}} and {{Q2|VAR}}. What is the total apparent power delivered by the source?
steps.explanation: Add powers as complex numbers: $P = {{P1}} + {{P2}}$ = {{P1+P2|W}} and $Q = {{Q1}} + ({{Q2}})$ = {{Q1+Q2|VAR}}. Then $|\mathbf{S}| = \sqrt{P^2 + Q^2}$ = {{sqrt((P1+P2)^2+(Q1+Q2)^2)|VA}}. Adding the separate apparent powers ({{sqrt(P1^2+Q1^2)+sqrt(P2^2+Q2^2)|VA}}) ignores that B's negative $Q$ partly cancels A's.

steps.prompt: A motor absorbs {{P|W}} from a {{V}} V rms line at a power factor of {{pf}} lagging. What rms current does it draw?
steps.explanation: $P = V_{rms}I_{rms}\cdot PF$, so $I_{rms} = \frac{P}{V_{rms}\,PF} = \frac{ {{P}} }{ {{V}}\times{{pf}} }$ = {{P/(V*pf)|A}}. At unity power factor it would only need {{P/V|A}}.

steps.prompt: A {{P|W}} load on a {{V}} V rms, {{f|Hz}} line has a power factor of {{pf1}} lagging. Which capacitance in parallel raises the power factor to {{pf2}} lagging?
Adding a capacitor in parallel with an inductive load changes the average power absorbed by the load.
steps.explanation: The load still sees the same voltage, so its current, $P$ and $Q$ are unchanged. The capacitor (which absorbs no average power) only supplies part of the load's reactive power locally, which reduces the **line** current.

steps.prompt: The graph shows the instantaneous power $p(t)$ absorbed by a load at 50 Hz.

ask.explanation: $p(t) = P + |\mathbf{S}|\cos(2\omega t + \dots)$ oscillates symmetrically around its average. Read $p_{max}$ = {{P+S|W}} and $p_{min}$ = {{P-S|W}}: $P = (p_{max} + p_{min})/2$ = {{P|W}}. The negative part means the load returns energy to the source for part of each cycle.

ask.prompt: Find the power factor of the load.
ask.explanation: Average: $P = (p_{max} + p_{min})/2$ = {{P|W}}. The oscillation amplitude is the apparent power: $|\mathbf{S}| = V_{rms}I_{rms} = (p_{max} - p_{min})/2$ = {{S|VA}}. So $PF = P/|\mathbf{S}|$ = {{cos(rad(th))}} (θ = {{th}}°).

steps.prompt: A source has $\mathbf{V}_t = {{Vt}}\angle 0^\circ$ V (peak) and $Z_t = {{Rt}} + j({{Xt}})$ Ω. Find the maximum average power it can deliver to a load $Z_L$ of any value.
steps.explanation:
Choose $Z_L = Z_t^* = {{Rt}} - j({{Xt}})$ Ω. The total impedance is $2R_t = {{2*Rt}}$ Ω, so $I_m = {{Vt}}/{{2*Rt}}$ = {{Vt/(2*Rt)|A}} and
$$P = \frac{I_m^2}{2}R_L = \frac{|\mathbf{V}_t|^2}{8R_t} = \frac{ {{Vt}}^2}{8\times{{Rt}} } = {{Vt^2/(8*Rt)}}\ \mathrm{W}$$

steps.prompt: A source has $Z_t = {{Rt}} + j{{Xt}}$ Ω. Which load impedance, of any value, absorbs the most average power?
steps.explanation: The optimum is the complex conjugate $Z_L = Z_t^* = {{Rt}} - j{{Xt}}$ Ω: the load reactance cancels the source reactance and $R_L = R_t$. ${{sqrt(Rt^2+Xt^2)}}$ Ω $= |Z_t|$ is only the best choice when the load must be purely resistive.

steps.prompt: A source with $\mathbf{V}_t = {{Vt}}\angle 0^\circ$ V (peak) and $Z_t = {{Rt}} + j{{Xt}}$ Ω drives the best possible **pure resistance** $R_L = |Z_t|$. Find the power delivered to $R_L$.
steps.explanation:
$R_L = |Z_t| = {{RL}}$ Ω. The loop impedance is $({{Rt}} + {{RL}}) + j{{Xt}}$ Ω, so $I_m = \frac{ {{Vt}} }{\sqrt{ {{Rt+RL}}^2 + {{Xt}}^2} }$ = {{Vt/sqrt((Rt+RL)^2+Xt^2)|A}}.
$P = \tfrac12 I_m^2R_L$ = {{0.5*Vt^2*RL/((Rt+RL)^2+Xt^2)|W}}, less than the conjugate-match maximum {{Vt^2/(8*Rt)|W}}.

steps.prompt: A {{P|W}} load on a {{V}} V rms line has PF = {{pf1}} lagging. After power-factor correction to {{pf2}}, what rms current does the line carry?
steps.explanation: $P$ is unchanged by the parallel capacitor, so $I_{rms} = \frac{P}{V_{rms}\,PF}$. Before: {{P/(V*pf1)|A}}. After: $\frac{ {{P}} }{ {{V}}\times{{pf2}} }$ = {{P/(V*pf2)|A}}, a reduction of {{100*(1-pf1/pf2)|%}}.

steps.prompt: A load connected to {{V}} V rms absorbs $\mathbf{S} = {{P}} + j({{Q}})$ VA. Model it as $Z = R + jX$ and find $R$.
A load connected to {{V}} V rms absorbs $\mathbf{S} = {{P}} + j({{Q}})$ VA. Model it as $Z = R + jX$ and find $X$ (with sign).
steps.explanation: $Z = \frac{V_{rms}^2}{\mathbf{S}^*} = \frac{V_{rms}^2(P + jQ)}{P^2 + Q^2}$, so $X = \frac{ {{V}}^2\times({{Q}})}{ {{P}}^2 + ({{Q}})^2}$ = {{V^2*Q/(P^2+Q^2)|Ω}}. The sign of $X$ follows the sign of $Q$: positive $Q$ means inductive.

steps.prompt: Put the steps for sizing a power-factor correction capacitor in order.
steps.explanation: $P$ stays the same, so the triangle shrinks only vertically. The capacitor must supply the difference in reactive power; its reactance follows from $Q_C = V_{rms}^2/X_C$, so $X_C < 0$, and then $C = 1/(\omega|X_C|)$.

steps.prompt: The graph shows the instantaneous power $p(t)$ absorbed by a load. What kind of load is it?
options: A load with both resistance and reactance
steps.explanation: $p(t)$ oscillates at twice the signal frequency around its average $P = |\mathbf{S}|\cos\theta$. If $p$ never goes negative and its minimum is 0, $\theta = 0$: a resistance. If it swings symmetrically around 0, $P = 0$ and $\theta = \pm 90^\circ$: a pure inductance or capacitance (you cannot tell which from $p(t)$ alone). In between ($0 < P < |\mathbf{S}|$, partly negative) the load has both R and X. Here $P$ = {{P|W}} and $|\mathbf{S}|$ = {{S|VA}}.
